notes.title: 2 Years surviving Game Dev and lessons from a Game Jam
notes.content:
[previewyoutube=XBAYj1HkXaU;full][/previewyoutube]
[b]Hey everyone! Welcome back to a new devlog![/b]
If you’re new here, I’m Dani Marti, and I’m making Lobo: The Howl Within—an action-adventure game with a strong story focus and intense combat.

I’ve been working on this game for a while now. The first devlog was [b]years ago[/b], and honestly, the journey hasn’t gotten any easier. I’m self-funding the project, which means I have to do freelance work—3D modeling, game development, whatever I can—to keep things going. A lot of indies have day jobs, so this isn’t anything new, but the last couple of years have been rough. Freelance work has been unpredictable, and I’ve been applying for jobs just to get some stability. 

I’m surviving, but some days feel like hitting rock bottom. I don’t want this to sound negative, but I also want to be real about the struggles of making an indie game.

[h2]Taking a Break with a Game Jam[/h2]
Back in January, I wasn’t feeling great, so I decided to take a small break and enter a tiny game jam. Sometimes stepping away from a big project helps you see things more clearly.

The jam theme was taxes (exciting, right?), so I made a meme game about a freelancer trying to file taxes on the last day before the IRS shuts down. And because it’s fantasy, a zombie apocalypse doesn’t stop them from making you pay.

It was a fun experience, and as always, I learned a lot.

[h2]What I Learned from the Game Jam[/h2]
[list]
[*] [b]We always overscope.[/b] Even in a two-week jam, I planned way too many features. In the end, I had to cut things just to finish, which affected the quality. Lesson learned: a small, polished game is always better than an ambitious but unfinished one. This made me rethink Lobo’s scope—I don’t want to spend the next 10 years making this game.
[*] [b]Level design is harder than it looks.[/b] I thought I could just throw in some assets, and boom—level done! Nope. Good level design tells a story, guides the player, and feels fun. And even after all that, it still needs to be optimized. Now, I’m designing small but meaningful levels and optimizing as I go, instead of waiting until the last minute.
[*] [b]Players will always do what you don’t expect.[/b] No matter how much effort you put into something, players will miss it, skip it, or speed-run it. The solution? Bottleneck key moments so they have to experience them.
[/list]

This game jam gave me fresh motivation to work on Lobo. I went back to my GDD, trimmed the scope, and simplified mechanics—without losing the game’s core identity. Long-term projects are all about trial, error, and commitment. It’s tempting to start something new when things get tough, but that’s usually a bigger mistake.

[h2]What’s New in Lobo?[/h2]

I’ve been focusing on the inventory system. I scrapped the old setup and rebuilt it using data assets instead of structures. Now, the inventory and equipment screens work together:
[list]
[*] Items show [b]detailed stats[/b] and attributes.
[*] If you have a similar item equipped, you get a [b]comparison view[/b].
[*] Everything is designed to be [b]fast and intuitive[/b]—less clicking, more playing.
[/list]
Right now, the game still looks like a prototype, but I’ll start using final assets soon.

[h2]That’s It for This Devlog![/h2]

I hope you found this update interesting or at least got something useful from it. Thanks for watching, and as always, see you in the next one!

Bye bye!

notes.title: Devlog 64: More Combat Features
notes.content:
[previewyoutube=UfuUxBga5Rc;full][/previewyoutube]

Hey everyone! Welcome back to another devlog for Lobo. 
For those who are new here, Lobo is an action-adventure game set in a fantasy world where humans and werewolves clash for survival. This month, I’ve been working on some exciting new features, including combat upgrades, UI improvements, and inventory updates. 

Let’s dive right in!

[h2]Stunning Enemies[/h2]
To add more variety to combat and encourage strategic play, you can now stun enemies with objects! This opens a short window to attack or make other moves. But be careful—some objects can break, making noise and attracting nearby enemies.

[h2]Spectator Camera[/h2]
Enemies now have a chance to perform synced animated attacks. To enhance the cinematic feel, I’ve added a dynamic spectator camera that frames the best angles during gameplay. It avoids obstacles, adjusts the lens, and adapts the field of view for a seamless experience. Behind the scenes, it uses a spring arm to avoid collisions and a line trace to find the best position, ensuring nothing interrupts the action.

[h2]Finishers[/h2]
Finishers are in! When an enemy’s health drops below a certain point and they’re in range, you can execute a finishing move. These moves, along with their range and health threshold, can be upgraded through the character’s skill tree. Each weapon also has unique finishers, making combat more dynamic and satisfying.

[h2]Counterattacks[/h2]
Combat now features counterattacks! If you time your block perfectly, you can strike back during an enemy’s attack. The timing window can be improved with character progression, giving you more room to master this skill.

[h2]UI Optimization[/h2]
I’ve optimized the inventory UI by combining all elements into a single material. Borders, backgrounds, icons, and states are now parameter-driven for better performance. For more UI tips, check out the talk "20 Things You Should Be Using in UMG"—link in [url=https://dev.epicgames.com/community/learning/talks-and-demos/MPZq/unreal-engine-20-things-you-should-be-using-in-unreal-motion-graphics-umg-unreal-fest-gold-coast-2024]here[/url]. 

[h2]Inventory and Equipment[/h2]
Quick update: I’ve added new inventory slots and improved equipment navigation. The camera now zooms in on the character for better inspection, and you can rotate them to view every detail.

[h2]Wrapping Up[/h2]
That’s it for this month! Thanks for tuning in. Subscribe for more updates, and don’t forget to wishlist Lobo on Steam to support the project.

notes.title: Devlog 62 - Applying D&D Theory Design to my Levels
notes.content:
[previewyoutube=NCva9uHBm2c;full][/previewyoutube]

Hey everyone! Welcome back to another devlog!

If you’re new here, I’m Dani Marti, and I’m working on Lobo, an action-adventure game inspired by The Last of Us, set in a fantasy world where humans and werewolves are in conflict. Combat’s a mix of melee and firearms – so yeah, things can get intense.

So, for the past few months, I’ve been all over the place. From the States to Europe, Asia, and now I’m in the UK. It’s been great, but it’s slowed down how often I can put out these devlogs and the game’s progress. Plus, I’m still feeling some burnout, and I’ve felt pretty stuck.

[h2]The Refactor[/h2]
The “stuck” feeling mainly comes from a huge refactor I’ve been doing. The combat system was buggy, so I decided to tear it down and start over. Lobo is pretty RPG-like, so all the systems are connected. When I pulled apart the combat system, everything kind of broke, and it was super overwhelming.

To handle that, I decided to split the project into two parts: one project for code, and one for level design. The code project is lightweight now, and the level design is just visual—assets, layout, all of that. This separation has been a lifesaver because I can jump into level design and vice-versa when I get frustrated with coding.

For the code issues, I set a goal to fix at least one thing every day. Some days, I knocked out a bunch of errors; other days, it was just one or two. But the important part was making progress. Slowly but surely, I started feeling excited about the project again as I chipped away at the bugs.

If you feel like me, I recommend breaking down your project into smaller parts and planning everything you can. Having my project in digestible pieces helped me immensely to recover from my burnout and get my excitement back.

[h2]Level Design[/h2]
If you’ve watched my previous devlogs, you know level design is something I struggle with. It’s harder than it looks—it’s not just about making something pretty. It must be fun to explore, guide the player, tell a story, and run smoothly.

I had a solid idea of what I wanted to do in terms of story, quests, and encounters, but the challenge was bringing it all together. So, I decided to start from scratch with a new approach. This time, I designed the entire first act of the game like a Dungeons & Dragons map. That means balancing exploration, encounters, and loot, so there’s always something to do—whether it’s fighting, finding lore, or looting.

Shoutout to Dungeon Masterpiece, who really inspired me to take this approach. If you’re into World Building, check out his videos—I’ll drop a link in the description.

Mapping out the whole level helped me see the flow of gameplay and keep the scope of Act 1 in check. It’s a big deal because it stops me from feeling overwhelmed and gives me a plan to follow, since Act 1 will be a public demo I will release in the following months. 

I started by blocking out the level with simple shapes to get the scale right. It’s quick to iterate, and I can jump in and playtest easily to make adjustments. I also used different colors to mark interactions like quests, fights, and cinematics. Seeing everything from a bird’s-eye view helps me balance the pacing of the level.

Next up is swapping out placeholders with actual models, adding detail, and setting up the lighting and mood—but that’s content for another devlog.

If you’re into Lobo, you can wishlist it now on Steam. Link’s in the description!
As always, thanks for watching, and I’ll catch you next time!

notes.title: Devlog 61 - Combat Token System, Comic Strip for Storytelling and much more!
notes.content:
[previewyoutube=50lAA2jVbpM;leftthumb][/previewyoutube]

Hi everyone!
Welcome to a new devlog!
In this episode, I will show the progress made this past month. This update includes:
[list]
[*] My token system for combat.
[*] My solution for storytelling.
[*] Using PCG for Level Design.
[*] Improvements in the spectator camera.
[*] New AI behaviors.
[*] Headshots.
[/list]
As you can see, there is lots of new stuff, so let's get started!

If you are new here, welcome! My name is Dani Marti, and I'm a solo developer creating an action-adventure game inspired by The Last of Us and Diablo.

[h2]Token System for Combat[/h2]
This system may look very complex, but it's much simpler than it seems. 
In my case, the Player and the Enemy are children classes from the same parent. So, since both will need a counter for tokens, I added the Combat Tokens variable to the parent. So I can access it from the children. In the same way, I added a new variable called Combat Tokens Max. This variable is hard-coded, but it could be different, for example, if I decide to have various difficulty levels. The hard-coded value is right now 2. That means that only two enemies will be able to attack at once.

On the Enemy side, there is a little more work; so let's see it step by step.

I'm using Behavior trees, and I have a task to perform the attack; if we take a look at the function, we will see that before attacking, we check if the attack is possible, so this is the perfect place to add a new condition, has the Player available tokens?

To answer this, I'm using a blueprint interface to improve the communication between the Player and the Enemy. Here, I have three functions, get the available tokens, consume tokens, and replenish tokens. This way, I can perform all the operations I need for the Enemy and the Player.

So, as you can see, the Enemy can perform Special Attacks, Finishers, and Normal Attacks. For Special and Normal Attacks, the Enemy only needs 1 token, but for Finishers, it uses 2; this is a way to ensure Finishers can be only performed by one Enemy at a time since finishers are synced animations and won't look good if more enemies are performing at the same time.

So, the first step is to check how many tokens the Player has available; in step 2, if there are enough tokens, the Enemy consumes the tokens from the Player. You can see the Consume and Replenish Token functions in action here.

The check fails if there aren't enough tokens and the Enemy circles the target. This behavior makes the Enemy look smarter since it looks like the Enemy moves to a better location to wait and try to attack again.

All the attacks are performed using Anim Montages, so after the Anim Montage is complete, we return the tokens from the Enemy to the Player, using the Consume and Replenish Tokens functions again.

The last thing to take into consideration is death. If an Enemy took Tokens from the Player, but we killed them before returning those Tokens, I forced the return in the Death Event. This way, other Enemies can still attack us.

That's how I created the system; the UI on top of the characters is just for debugging and making it more visual.
Please let me know in the comments below if you have any questions about the system.

[h2]Dynamic Comic Strip[/h2]
The next significant feature is the Dynamic Comic Strip.
I created this feature because I'm creating an adventure game, and this kind of game usually has tons of cinematics. Since I'm not an animator, and my expectations are over the top due to my annoying perfectionism. I knew that would take too long, and I probably wouldn't be happy with the results. So, I came up with this system:
[list]
[*] I have several Scene Capture Cameras in the scene that frame what will be shown in the comic strip.
[*] Each camera has a post-process effect with the hatching style and the outline.
[*] I use the Custom Depth pass to choose what elements are displayed in color.
[*] All is displayed as UI.
[/list]

If you are interested in the system, I can go for a deeper dive in another devlog, but this is, so far, the overview.

A couple things worth mentioning, I'm not a shader artist by any means; so for my shader, I created a mix using tutorials from [url=https://youtu.be/3Q6Ik1V75I8]Visual Tech Art [/url]and [url=https://youtu.be/18U50KPdD2A]Kamil Hepner[/url]. They are very good tutorials and worth checking out.

The other thing is that I find the animation UI system very annoying and hard to manipulate. So, I created a blueprint assistant that manages the UI animations using timelines; this way, I can just manipulate the times and curves more efficiently, which allows for a very fast iteration.

For my UI and animations, I used the UI materials from the [url=https://www.unrealengine.com/marketplace/en-US/product/ui-material-lab]UI Material Lab[/url], which is a free resource from Unreal Engine. The information there is pure gold. 

The last thing I want to mention is that the system initially fed the comic stripes with render target textures, so the caption was done in real-time. 

After some testing, I realized the rendering of three images simultaneously was dropping my fps considerably, so now I'm manually rendering and saving the images beforehand. It's not so convenient, but it's much more performant since I'm just dealing with textures and UI now.

[h2]Using PCG for Level Design[/h2]
If you have been watching my devlogs, you know how much I struggle with my level design. Step by step, I'm getting more comfortable and coming up with my own solutions. For me, one of the biggest challenges is creating boundaries that limit the Player's movement.

I found [url=https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLB7VoDymYuMQWMPdWQv5CszLD30taMnGc]Blaze 92[/url], a youtube channel that showcases games and how they overcome that challenge. Very interesting and inspirational to apply to your games. 

So why creating boundaries is a challenge? In my case, I want the boundaries to be and feel natural, i'm not creating an open world, but I want the Player to have 'certain' freedom to move around. And when you do that, the dangers are:
[list]
[*] The Player can feel lost.
[*] The Player has more freedom to do things you didn't expect, which is always very dangerous.
[*] It's harder to direct the Player towards goals and quests.
[/list]

So, after some research, I decided to limit my level using geographical boundaries such as cliffs and rock formations. And when the level is flatter, I use what I call Forest walls; those are dense and have higher bushes, which show the Player that they can't go through, just like you wouldn't go through in real life. To add and manipulate those boundaries, I created a PCG Spline tool that allows me to easily make them.

On the other hand, I'm populating my forest using PCG based on landscape materials; this is super useful because I just need to paint my landscape with different materials to populate different assets. If you are into PCG, I highly recommend you check Aziel Arts's tutorials; for me, the best PCG tutorials on Youtube. He has a [url=https://youtu.be/G_uIWC6-RsM?si=fuV-tUNQ1kZUFvND]tutorial[/url] about populating landscapes.


[h2]Other updates[/h2]
Last but not least, I made some improvements in my Spectator Camera, so now, the camera is always consistent with the framing, that means for example if the Enemy was coming from the left, the spectator camera keeps that framing so the Player and the Enemy are in the same position. That can seem silly, but because the camera now has collisions and detects nearby objects, it could pick a better location with fewer collisions, switching the frame, which doesn't look good. Now, the camera keeps the framing and adjusts the focal length to fit all the actors in the frame.

On the other hand, AI now shares core behaviors for different enemy types, such as discovering dead fellas and warning other enemies.

I also improved the aiming and shooting system, including headshots, which are very satisfactory.

So that was all the progress since the last devlog. I hope you like it.
On the other hand, Lobo is on Steam, so please don't forget to add it to your wishlist if you like it, and if you want to support me further, I created a [url=https://ko-fi.com/danimarti]Ko-fi[/url] page where you have special perks and exclusive content. 


As always, thanks so much for watching and see you in the next devlog! Bye bye!

notes.title: Devlog 60 - Combat Updates, Level Blockout and many news in Lobo
notes.content:
Hi everyone! Welcome to a new devlog!
If you are new here, my name is Dani Marti, and I'm developing an action-adventure game inspired by The Last of Us and Diablo in Unreal Engine 5.

[previewyoutube=csKeaYEGOCU;full][/previewyoutube]

This devlog took a bit longer than usual, basically, for two reasons:

[h3]1- Burnout[/h3]
I never got burnt out in seven years of game development. For the last month, I wanted to work on my game, but my productivity was so low; no matter how many hours I was forcing myself to be in front of the computer, nothing was happening. When I don't progress, I can get demotivated, and that can lead to a vicious cycle. 
So, I decided to take a break and return to the game with fresh eyes and new ideas.

[h3]2- Moving[/h3]
We had to move from Maui to Barcelona temporarily. This is just for a few months, but that meant moving everything to storage and making all the arrangements to live in a different country for several months, which didn't leave much time to work on my game.

[h2]So where is the game now? [/h2]
Well, the game is now in its fourth refactoring. Remember months ago when I said the last refactoring would be the last one? I was wrong.
And then, Besides the refactoring, I decided to do some game redesign:
[olist]
[*] I'm reducing the scope of the game. I decided to reduce some of the features that I can't do by myself or would take too long. That affects mainly cinematics and combat. However, I have come up with a solution that will allow me to tell the story in a way that will not require much development time. I will go deeper into detail about this in another devlog. 
[*] The second thing is the combat. I'm changing the complexity of the combat slightly because I don't have all the animations I would like, so I would need to hire an animator. This is a minor change that affects more the aesthetics than the mechanics. I'm trying to reshape all my limitations to make a better game.
[/olist]

On the other hand, I introduced a new stance, gun and sword; I think this stance can be very fun for the player to develop a different gameplay than the traditional stances. 

I'm focusing on making the combat fun, smooth, and very good-looking; the quality is very important to me, so I prefer a slightly simpler combat that feels great than a more complex but clunky one.

Part of the refactoring is improving and optimizing the animation system; for example, all the characters share the same skeleton and animation blueprint, and their blueprints are children from the same parent. 

Lastly, I'm remaking the Enemy AI from scratch, improving their behaviors and making them more interesting and smart. Enemies can spot dead fellas, warn other enemies, investigate hidden spots, and, of course, block and dodge our attacks so each encounter is more meaningful and challenging.

Regarding Level Design, I'm back to the basics, blocking out my levels; I have been watching tons of tutorials and courses to design fun levels that convey the story and gameplay, something that's not easy at all. We will have a new level very soon.

On the other hand, I started a [url=https://ko-fi.com/danimarti/]ko-fi page[/url], so if you want to support the game, get special updates, and be part of it, you can now.

And that's all for now... as always, thanks so much for watching; see you soon!
